policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R2. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R3. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R4. If no multiple support agreement is mentioned, assume there is none.
R5. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year, unless the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R6. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R7. If a joint return is not described as filed only for a refund, assume it is not.
R8. The person may not file a joint return for the year, unless the joint return is filed only to claim a refund of withheld tax.
case_text: Case file summary for dependent claim on 2026 return 2093, submitted by Daniel Nguyen. The taxpayer inquired about submitting the tax documents electronically. By relationship, the person is the taxpayer's brother or sister. The individual is designated on the return solely under the qualifying child standard. The individual resided in the taxpayer's household for a period of 7 months during the tax year. Wage earnings reported on Form W-2 for the individual total $1,500. Citizenship status confirms the individual is a citizen of the United States. The tax professional noted an early submission to expedite the expected refund. Medical documentation from a physician certifies the individual as permanently and totally disabled. The taxpayer reached the age of 23 by the close of the tax year. Personal financial contributions funded 40% of the individual's total annual support. The joint return was submitted for purposes exceeding a mere recovery of withheld income taxes. Outside of financial matters, the individual performs in a local community orchestra on weekends. Supporting relatives executed a multiple support agreement designating the taxpayer as the claimant. No alternative taxpayer is eligible to claim the individual as a qualifying child. Enrollment records show the individual maintained full-time student status for a minimum of 5 months. Financial institutions credited the individual with $500 in taxable interest earnings. The individual attained the age of 23 by the end of the year. Gross income figures totaling $4,400 incorporate wages, taxable interest, and rental receipts prior to deductions. An external taxpayer maintains the right to claim the taxpayer as a dependent for this period. Absences from the primary residence were temporary educational departures while maintaining the individual's permanent room. The taxpayer engaged a commercial tax preparation service for the first time. The age difference between the taxpayer and the individual is 0 years. Legal adoption proceedings between the taxpayer and the individual have not occurred. A properly executed Form 8332 releasing claim rights from the custodial parent is included with the filing. The taxpayer provided 100% of the financial support expended on behalf of the individual. Neither biological nor legal parent is attempting to claim the individual. Gross rental collections from a tenant amounted to $2,400 before accounting for expenses.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R2. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more).
R3. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico. This rule does not apply if the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.
R4. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support.
R5. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R6. If the return does not say the person is another taxpayer's qualifying child, assume they are not.
R7. A qualifying relative's gross income, which counts wages, taxable interest and rent received before expenses, must be less than $5,300.
R8. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
case_text: Case file entry for return 4877 for the tax year 2026, submitted by filer Daniel Nguyen regarding dependent eligibility. Financial records show that Daniel contributed 45% toward the individual's total annual support. Investigations confirm that no other filer claims this individual as a qualifying child. The intake documents indicate no reported disability for the individual. Employment records indicate wages earned by the individual totaled $1,500. Records confirm that no biological or legal parent is attempting to claim the individual. The filer, Daniel, can be claimed as a dependent on their own parents' tax return. The married couple filed a joint return solely to recover withheld income taxes. Daniel attained the age of 66 by the close of the 2026 tax year. Official adoption documentation shows the individual was legally adopted by Daniel, who holds United States citizenship. Academic transcripts verify full-time enrollment spanning at least 5 calendar months in 2026. Bank statements attribute $250 in taxable interest income to the individual. No Form 8332 release has been executed or filed. Residency logs establish that the individual resided in Daniel's household for a full 12 months. Agency placement papers designate the individual as a foster child placed by an authorized organization. No multiple support agreement was executed for this household. Periods spent away from the residence were due to educational attendance, with living quarters maintained continuously for the individual. The individual frequently prepares meals for the household members during weekends. Rental income collected by the individual amounted to $0, excluding property maintenance expenses. Household members participate in weekly religious services at a nearby church. The individual is not filing a joint return with any spouse. Combining wages, interest, and pre-expense rental receipts, the individual's gross income totals $1,750. A comparison of birth dates shows the filer is older than the individual by 43 years. The individual provided 40% of their own financial support throughout the year. The individual reached the age of 23 by the end of the tax year. The individual holds citizenship and residency in Brazil, and not in the United States, Canada, or Mexico.

A comparison of birth dates shows the taxpayer is older than the dependent by 3 years. Residence records demonstrate the dependent maintained a shared household with the taxpayer for a total of 7 months. Financial ledgers indicate that 100% of the dependent's overall financial maintenance was provided by the taxpayer. Enrollment documentation confirms the dependent maintained full-time student status during a span of 5 months within the calendar year. The dependent and their spouse submitted a joint tax return for the year 2026. Household notes remark that the individual frequently assists with domestic chores. Leisure activities for the individual involve participating in a regional weekend orchestra. Form 1099 records show the individual accrued $500 in taxable interest. The case file contains no executed Form 2120 agreements from any secondary contributors. At the close of the tax year, the taxpayer had reached the age of 26. Weekly schedules for the household typically include attending services at the neighborhood house of worship. Gross rental payments collected by the individual amounted to $1,200 prior to accounting for maintenance expenses. Logistical logs establish that the dependent resided elsewhere during the remaining months under permanent, non-temporary arrangements. Legal records confirm the individual was never formally adopted by the taxpayer. Medical and personal history forms indicate the individual does not have a qualifying disability. The assigned tax professional has maintained a longstanding advisory relationship with the household. The joint filing was submitted to address overall tax liability rather than merely claiming a refund of excess withholdings. The taxpayer is not claimed as a dependent on any other individual's tax filing. Verification checks verify that no other filer lists this individual as a qualifying child. Independent financial calculations show the individual funded 20% of their living expenses using personal earnings.

A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. The person may not file a joint return for the year.
R2. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico. This rule does not apply if the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.
R3. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R4. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R5. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R6. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R7. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R8. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support.
R9. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more).
case_text: Case file summary for Jamal Washington regarding dependent status claimed on return 7081 for the 2026 tax year. Form W-2 records report wage earnings of $6,000 for the individual. The individual resided at the taxpayer's residence for a duration of 4 months during 2026. Reported taxable interest income for the individual totals $0. No Form 2120 multiple support declaration was executed by any other contributing party. The individual is a U.S. citizen who was legally adopted by the taxpayer. Enrollment records confirm the individual was not enrolled as a full-time student for any 5-month period during the year. The taxpayer designates the individual as a dependent under qualifying child provisions. The individual provided 80% of their total annual support using their personal earnings. The individual's physical absence was temporary due to hospitalization, with an anticipated return to the household. The taxpayer contributed 50% toward the aggregate support provided for the individual. Outside of personal finances, the individual performs in a local musical ensemble on weekends. The individual is not filing a joint return with a spouse. Another taxpayer lists the individual as their qualifying child. The age difference between the taxpayer and the individual is -18 years. The individual's total gross income, comprising wages, taxable interest, and unreduced rent receipts, amounts to $6,000. The joint return is submitted solely to claim a refund of withheld taxes, with no tax liability and no credit claims. Taxpayer engagement records note the utilization of a paid tax professional for the initial filing season. Gross rental income received by the individual before maintenance deductions is $0. The taxpayer attained the age of 50 as of the close of the tax year. Genealogical records establish that the individual is related to the taxpayer as a cousin. An independent taxpayer is eligible to claim the taxpayer as a dependent for the current year. No Form 8332 release of claim to exemption has been signed. Medical documentation indicates the individual does not meet disability criteria. The individual reached 68 years of age by the end of 2026. The individual holds citizenship and residency in Brazil rather than the United States, Canada, or Mexico. The biological parents of the individual have not claimed them on any tax return.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R2. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.
R3. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
R4. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R5. If the return does not say the person is another taxpayer's qualifying child, assume they are not.
R6. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R7. The person may not file a joint return for the year.
R8. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R9. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support. This rule does not apply if a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
case_text: Jamal Washington is preparing his 2026 federal income tax return, assigned file number 9790. The individual is not claimed as a qualifying child on any other taxpayer's return. According to the attached W-2 form, the individual earned wages totaling $6,000. Documentation indicates the individual provided 60% of their total financial support throughout the year. In their spare time, the individual enjoys preparing weekend meals for everyone living in the house. Financial records show that the taxpayer contributed 45% toward the individual's total maintenance and care. The taxpayer frequently mentions how much assistance the individual provides with daily household chores. The joint return is submitted to claim benefits beyond simply recovering taxes withheld from pay. Official school transcripts confirm full-time academic enrollment for at least 5 separate calendar months in 2026. The taxpayer cannot be claimed as a dependent on the tax return of any other filer. The individual reached 23 years of age by the close of 2026. A licensed physician has officially certified the individual as having a permanent and total disability. Musical activities keep the individual busy as they play instruments in a local community orchestra on weekends. Form 8332 was properly executed and signed by the custodial parent to release the exemption claim to the taxpayer. Form 1099 records reflect that the individual received $500 in taxable interest income. One of the biological parents has also listed the individual as a qualifying child on their tax filing for this year. The contributing relatives executed a multiple support agreement designating the taxpayer to claim the exemption. During the remaining months, the individual resided elsewhere under circumstances that do not qualify as a temporary absence. The individual holds status as a citizen of the United States. There is no legal adoption relationship established between the taxpayer and the individual. The taxpayer reached the age of 35 by the end of the tax year. Household residency logs establish that the individual lived in the taxpayer's residence for all 12 months of 2026. The individual is related to the taxpayer as a mother-in-law or father-in-law. For the first time, the taxpayer has decided to hire a professional tax preparer to handle the filing. The individual collected $0 in rental payments, excluding any amounts designated for property upkeep. The taxpayer is pursuing the dependency claim under the provisions for a qualifying relative. The taxpayer is older than the individual by a margin of 12 years. Combining wages, taxable interest, and gross rental receipts before deductions yields a total gross income of $6,500 for the individual.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year, unless the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R2. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R3. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R4. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R5. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R6. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R7. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support. This rule does not apply if a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R8. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.

The professional assisting the taxpayer has maintained a longstanding relationship with the household. Documentation includes a properly executed Form 8332 provided by the custodial parent. The file contains no multiple support agreement for the individual. A comparison of birth dates shows a 31-year age difference between the taxpayer and the individual. The individual is not designated as a qualifying child on any other taxpayer's filing. Family lineage connects the individual to the taxpayer as a father-in-law or mother-in-law. Enrollment records verify that the individual attended school full-time for at least 5 months during the year. Financial records establish that the taxpayer provided 75% of the total support for the individual. Financial institution statements report $0 of taxable interest paid to the individual. The joint return is submitted for purposes extending beyond the mere recovery of withheld taxes. Periods away from the residence constituted temporary educational absences, with personal living quarters maintained. Medical documentation includes a physician's certification of permanent and total disability for the individual. Personal earnings accounted for 80% of the individual's total financial support. The taxpayer cannot be claimed as a dependent on the return of any other filer. Gross rental collections from property tenants amounted to $0 prior to expense deductions. The taxpayer attained the age of 50 by the close of the tax year. Members of the household participate in weekly services at the neighborhood church. The individual maintained a primary residence in the taxpayer's home for 6 months throughout 2026. Neither biological nor adoptive parents of the individual are attempting to claim them.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R2. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R3. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R4. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R5. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R6. If no multiple support agreement is mentioned, assume there is none.
R7. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R8. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support. This rule does not apply if a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R9. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support. This rule does not apply if a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R2. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.
R3. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R4. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R5. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R6. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R7. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R8. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R9. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.

Documentation includes a Form 2120 multiple support declaration designating the taxpayer. Gross rent collected by the individual totaled $1,200 prior to factoring in upkeep costs. Sunday services at a local church are a regular part of the family's routine. A difference of 44 years separates the age of the taxpayer from that of the individual. The custodial parent has chosen not to release the claim via Form 8332.

R9. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R10. If a joint return is not described as filed only for a refund, assume it is not.

policy_text:

A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R8. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico, unless the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R2. If the return does not say the person is another taxpayer's qualifying child, assume they are not.
R3. A taxpayer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent may not claim any dependent.
R4. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico, unless the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.
R5. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support. This rule does not apply if a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R6. If the return does not say someone else can claim the taxpayer, assume no one can.
R7. A qualifying relative's gross income, which counts wages, taxable interest and rent received before expenses, must be less than $5,300.
R8. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more), unless the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R2. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R3. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R4. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R5. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R6. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R7. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R8. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico. This rule does not apply if the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.
